Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 5
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Explanation

The application is setting the server port. To migrate a Java application that sets the server port to Azure Container Apps:

*Azure Container Apps allows you to expose port according to your Azure Container Apps resource configuration. For instance, a Spring Boot application listens to port of 8080 by default, but it can be set with server.port or environment variable SERVER_PORT as you need.
Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that is not the latest stable release.
Upgrading to the latest stable version ensures you benefit from the newest features, performance improvements, bug fixes, and security patches. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest stable version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose the latest stable Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and identify the latest stable release.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java 21 Spring Boot application for browsing, uploading, viewing, and deleting photos. This source-based assessment describes the current implementation and Docker Compose topology; it does not imply a verified live deployment.

Application Architecture

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the sole application datastore. The Photo entity maps UUID identifiers, original filenames, MIME types, file sizes, timestamps, dimensions, and binary image data to photos; photo_data is a JPA large-object field. Uploads are stored in the database and served through /photo/{id}, not written to the bundled static/uploads directory. Compose persists Oracle files in oracle_data, mounts initialization scripts, and waits for database health before starting the application on the shared bridge network. Both default and Docker profiles configure Hibernate ddl-auto=create, so application startup recreates the mapped schema despite volume persistence. Database and administrator credentials are externally supplied; credential values are intentionally omitted.

The browser retrieves Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr. No server-side external API, object-storage service, cache, message broker, or external identity provider is evident in the inspected implementation. H2 is declared only as a test-scoped dependency, not the configured runtime datastore.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A layered monolith uses constructor injection from MVC controllers through the PhotoService interface to its transactional implementation and a Spring Data repository. There is no separate networked business service.
  • Images and metadata share Oracle persistence. Gallery ordering and adjacent-photo navigation use native Oracle SQL, including NVL, ROWNUM, and SYSDATE, tying repository behavior to Oracle.
  • Read endpoints are public; upload and delete POST endpoints require authentication. SecurityConfig builds an in-memory administrator with BCrypt, enables stateless HTTP Basic, and disables CSRF. The inspected server configuration exposes HTTP; no TLS termination is defined here.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicit HTTP endpoint mappings expose gallery browsing, multipart uploads, image retrieval, and deletion. Browser requests and persistence calls are synchronous; uploads return JSON while gallery/detail requests render HTML.

Service Catalog

ServicePortCategoryPurpose

There is one Maven module and one independently deployable source-built application. Key dependencies are Spring Boot 3.5.0 Web/MVC, Thymeleaf, Data JPA, Validation, Security, Jackson through the JSON starter, and the Oracle JDBC driver. Oracle is a prebuilt image, not a source module. No gateway, discovery server, observability service, Kubernetes deployment, or Helm chart was found in the tracked deployment artifacts.

API Endpoints Inventory

Paths are unversioned: no URL, header, or query-based version scheme was found. All mappings belong to photoalbum-java-app; there are no explicit PUT, PATCH, or DELETE mappings. Deletion uses POST.

Service / ControllerMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
App / HomeController.indexGET/No declared parameters or body200 HTML index view with List model; loading errors produce an empty gallery rather than an error status.
App / HomeController.uploadPhotosPOST/uploadmultipart/form-data, repeated required files parts bound to List; HTTP Basic authentication200 JSON Map containing success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads, including partial or complete per-file failure; 400 JSON for an empty list or handled multipart exception; 401 without valid authentication.
App / DetailController.detailGET/detail/{id}String path parameter identifying a photo200 HTML detail view with a Photo and previous/next navigation IDs; 302 redirect to / for blank/missing photo or caught exception.
App / DetailController.deletePhotoPOST/detail/{id}/deleteString path parameter; no body DTO required; HTTP Basic authentication302 redirect to / with success/error flash message, including not-found and caught deletion failures; 401 without valid authentication.
App / PhotoFileController.servePhotoGET/photo/{id}String path parameter; browser cache-busting query parameters are not bound by the controller200 ResponseEntity backed by ByteArrayResource, content type from stored photo MIME type; 404 for blank ID, absent photo, or empty binary data; 500 for caught exceptions.

Upload response handling distinguishes transport failure from item failure: clients must inspect the JSON result even after HTTP 200. A successful service upload is followed by a metadata lookup; only a present photo is added to the success list. Exceptions escaping service transaction completion or this lookup are not covered by a general upload-controller exception handler, so the normal JSON envelope is not guaranteed for every server error.

Image responses explicitly send Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size. No download-disposition header is set.

Framework-provided static resource handling serves assets such as /css/site.css and /js/upload.js; these are not additional business-controller mappings. Spring Boot's conventional /error handling is framework infrastructure, not a custom API contract.

There are no gateway-level aggregation DTOs or separate backend-service contracts. Entity field and persistence documentation belongs in data-architecture.md; validation details belong in business-workflows.md.

Jackson supplied by Spring Boot serializes the upload maps, including metadata timestamps. No custom serializer, Jackson configuration, OpenAPI/Swagger specification or annotations, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was found in the application artifacts. HTML rendering uses Thymeleaf. A successful upload response is a metadata projection, not an image payload; clients fetch the binary separately.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-155; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-47; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:58-97; pom.xml:31-47,75-79.

Communication Patterns

  • Browser to application: Same-origin HTTP requests, form submissions, and image loads. upload.js uses browser fetch with FormData. Its JavaScript async/await is not asynchronous service messaging: the HTTP response waits for upload processing.
  • Inside the application: Controllers call PhotoService directly; PhotoServiceImpl calls PhotoRepository synchronously. Uploads process files sequentially, persist each photo, then retrieve its metadata. Detail rendering composes a photo and adjacent-photo navigation through local service calls, not gateway aggregation.
  • External dependency: JPA/JDBC communicates with Oracle over its database protocol. Compose resolves the database by service hostname; standalone configuration targets a local database by default. There is no REST client, gRPC client, message broker, event bus, pub/sub, application service registry, or client-side load balancer.
  • Browser-only external assets: Templates reference Bootstrap assets on jsDelivr over HTTPS. This is a browser CDN dependency, not a backend service call.
  • Resilience: No application retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, or explicit outbound request/query timeout policy was found. Framework/driver defaults are not an explicit service-level guarantee. Container restart-on-failure is a process policy, not a request retry. Gallery read errors fall back to an empty HTML gallery; detail errors redirect; deletion errors redirect with a flash message; image-serving errors return 500. Per-file upload failures generally become failure entries in a 200 response; there is no distributed compensation or fallback backend.
  • Availability: In Compose, the application depends on database readiness. Database unavailability affects operations; full startup configuration belongs in configuration-inventory.md.
  • Authentication and authorization: Stateless HTTP Basic authentication protects POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete. An in-memory user has an ADMIN role, but route rules require only authentication, not a role check. Remaining requests are permitted by the security rules. Missing/invalid credentials on protected operations result in 401, with an HTTP Basic challenge. No JWT, OAuth2, form-login endpoint, or method-level authorization is implemented. CSRF protection is explicitly disabled.
  • Transport: No application HTTPS/TLS listener, TLS enforcement, or TLS-terminating reverse proxy is configured in the inspected deployment files. HTTP Basic therefore requires deployment-level TLS for secure credential transport. Database transport encryption is not explicitly configured. Credentials are externally supplied; no credential values are reproduced here.
  • Client behavior: The upload script does not construct an Authorization header or provide its own login flow; protected operations need an authenticated browser HTTP Basic context or an API client supplying credentials.

Service Communication Sequence

The upload flow illustrates authentication, sequential synchronous processing, item-level rejection, and subsequent public image retrieval. Dashed arrows denote replies, not broker messaging.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose interpolation → requires all three supplied password variables before service creation.
  2. oracle-db → Oracle startup/init scripts → application schema credentials and grants. 01-create-user.sh creates the user if absent and applies schema-oriented grants without DBA; create-user.sh additionally has a fixed sleep 30, not a readiness polling loop.
  3. Oracle health check → authenticated SQLPlus invocation using APP_USER and APP_USER_PASSWORD, with inline SELECT 1 FROM DUAL; piped to SQLPlus and shell || exit 1. Interval 30s, timeout 10s, retries 15, start period 180s. Compose escapes variable expansion with $$ so references resolve inside the container. No explicit SQL error-exit directive is configured, so the supplied check should not be assumed to validate every SQL error through its process status. The separate healthcheck.sql contains a similar query but is not referenced by the Compose health command.
  4. photoalbum-java-app → waits for oracle-db via Compose depends_on: condition: service_healthy; then starts Java with the Docker profile. There is no explicit application health check, readiness probe, config-server retry, or application startup timeout setting.

02-verify-user.sql checks the literal default schema identifier rather than deriving it from APP_USER, which matters when that variable is changed. Mounted startup scripts are image-managed; no additional explicit inter-script orchestration is declared in Compose.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  1. Operator copies .env.example to ignored .env, replaces all three placeholder passwords with unique values, or supplies equivalent shell environment variables.
  2. Compose checks required values and binds the Oracle administrator credential to the database container only; the application schema password is shared by the database initialization and application datasource. The administrator login password is supplied to the Java application.
  3. Initialization scripts authenticate to Oracle as SYSDBA using the administrator credential and create/configure the schema account with scoped creation privileges and tablespace quota. No cloud identity/RBAC provisioning is present.
  4. Spring resolves datasource and administrator password properties from the application environment. SecurityConfig BCrypt-encodes the administrator password into an in-memory user store.
  5. Tests substitute test-classpath credentials. No automated secret retrieval, rotation, deployment identity workflow, Docker Secrets, or Kubernetes Secrets is supplied.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared photo collection and navigate individual images. Authenticated operators can add photos in batches and permanently remove photos.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhoto managementA stored image with descriptive information used for gallery display and chronological navigation. The only persisted business entity.Combines image content and metadata; related to neighboring photos through upload chronology, not explicit associations.
UploadResultPhoto intakeTransient outcome of an individual upload, not a persisted entity or aggregate.Identifies a successfully created Photo or associates an error with the submitted filename.

There is no persisted Album, User, ownership relationship, tagging system, or explicit DDD aggregate model. The gallery is a view over the shared Photo collection.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-10.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application, not a set of independently deployed business services. The following rows describe internal responsibilities.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplPhoto intake, browsing, and removalPhoto lifecycle; UploadResult outcomesPhotoRepository and the configured database; image-header inspection
HomeControllerGallery presentation and batch intake orchestrationNone; composes Photo summaries and upload outcomesPhotoService
DetailControllerIndividual photo browsing and removalNone; composes current photo and navigation referencesPhotoService
PhotoFileControllerImage deliveryNone; serves Photo contentPhotoService

PhotoService is the application-level authority for photo changes; the database stores both original image bytes and metadata. Controllers share that authority rather than maintaining separate domain copies.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-46; controller constructors; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-59.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch and update the gallery

  1. The visitor selects or drops files. The browser applies Client intake checks, submits eligible files to POST /upload, and displays progress.
  2. The security boundary requires Mutation authorization before the controller processes the batch.
  3. HomeController applies Batch presence and then calls PhotoService once per submitted file, in sequence.
  4. PhotoService applies Server intake checks, reads the image bytes, and attempts Image dimension inspection.
  5. An accepted file becomes a Photo with an identity and upload time, then is saved with its content. A rejected file produces an unsuccessful UploadResult without intentionally creating a Photo.
  6. For a successful result, HomeController reads the saved Photo back to compose its gallery summary. Rejections become filename/error entries.
  7. The controller returns combined successful and failed outcomes under Batch outcome semantics. The browser prepends successful photo cards and displays returned failures; each card subsequently fetches its image separately.

This is partial-success batch orchestration, not an all-or-nothing batch transaction. Earlier successful uploads are not compensated if a later file fails. A readback exception can abort the response after photos have already been committed.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-158; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:56-107; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:80-184.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and navigate a photo

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController requests all photos through PhotoService and renders the gallery using Gallery ordering.
  2. If retrieval fails, the controller logs the failure and renders an empty collection. The same empty-gallery prompt appears for a genuinely empty collection; no stale collection is supplied.
  3. Opening GET /detail/{id} loads the selected Photo, then queries older and newer photos through Chronological navigation. The view combines photo information with available neighbor links.
  4. Invalid, missing, or failed detail retrieval redirects to the gallery; a failure in either neighbor lookup also takes this path.
  5. The browser separately requests GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController applies Content availability, retrieves stored bytes, and serves the original content. It does not generate a thumbnail or transformed image.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:38-50; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-87; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-94.

Workflow 3: Permanently remove a photo

  1. The detail-page deletion form asks for browser confirmation before submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete.
  2. After Mutation authorization, DetailController calls PhotoService.
  3. PhotoService looks up the Photo. If absent, it returns false; otherwise, it removes the stored Photo, including its content.
  4. The controller sets a success, not-found, or failure flash message and redirects to the gallery.

There is no soft-delete, recycle bin, approval step, or restore workflow. Browser confirmation is a presentation safeguard, not a server-side approval requirement.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-209.

No scheduled business jobs, event listeners, message consumers, CLI business commands, or business-data initialization routines were found in the inspected application sources. The application entry point only starts the application (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14).

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no inter-service business calls, gateway aggregation endpoints, domain events, or circuit breakers. All composition occurs inside the application:

  • Upload composition: browser files → HomeController → PhotoService → PhotoRepository/database; accepted photo IDs are read back into summaries and combined with per-file failures. The browser joins image URLs and detail links to summaries using the Photo identity.
  • Detail composition: DetailController combines the current Photo with older/newer lookup results from the same repository. Only navigation identities are added to the view; no other domain owns this information.
  • Content delivery: gallery/detail markup references image identities; subsequent browser requests obtain bytes from that same persisted Photo. There is no external object-storage handoff.
  • Degradation: gallery read failure yields an empty gallery, detail failure redirects home, missing/empty image content yields not-found, and unexpected image-delivery errors yield a server error. Upload failures are normally reported per file; there is no alternate storage or queued retry. Browser request failures show a generic retry message.

Evidence: HomeController.java:69-97, DetailController.java:39-57, PhotoFileController.java:46-86 under src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:102-132,176-179.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram actor Operator participant Browser as "Gallery browser" participant Access as "Access control" participant Intake as "Batch intake controller" participant Service as "Photo management" participant Photo as "Photo" participant Store as "Photo repository and database" Operator->>Browser: Select or drop photos Browser->>Browser: Apply client intake checks Browser->>Access: Submit eligible files alt Request is not authenticated Access-->>Browser: Reject mutation request Browser-->>Operator: Show upload failure else Request is authenticated Access->>Intake: Process submitted batch Intake->>Intake: Require at least one file loop Each file in a nonempty batch Intake->>Service: Add photo Service->>Service: Apply server intake and dimension rules alt File is rejected or cannot be read Service-->>Intake: Failed file outcome else File is eligible Service->>Photo: Create photo with available dimensions Service->>Store: Save photo and original content alt Persistence succeeds Store-->>Service: Saved photo Service-->>Intake: Successful photo identity Intake->>Service: Retrieve saved photo summary Service->>Store: Find saved photo Store-->>Service: Photo Service-->>Intake: Gallery summary else Persistence reports failure Service-->>Intake: Failed file outcome when handled end end end Intake-->>Browser: Combined outcomes or empty batch error Browser-->>Operator: Add accepted cards and show errors end

The diagram shows normal handled outcomes. Transaction-commit failures and summary-readback exceptions can escape per-file handling; the browser then receives a request-level failure rather than a complete batch report.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Intake and validation

  • Client intake checks: browser MIME allowlist accepts JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP; each selected file must be no larger than 10 MiB. Rejected files are excluded from submission. These checks do not replace server validation.
  • Batch presence: null or empty file lists yield a bad-request response with a no-files error. The controller maps MultipartException to the same generic error.
  • Server intake checks: the declared MIME type, lowercased, must match the configured allowlist; content must be nonempty and no larger than the configured maximum, currently 10,485,760 bytes. Missing MIME metadata triggers generic failure handling rather than a dedicated validation message. There is no explicit content-signature agreement check.
  • Image dimension inspection: a recognized image reader inspects the first image's dimensions without fully decoding it. More than 40,000,000 pixels is rejected. No available reader or a non-I/O inspection exception permits continuation without dimensions; an IOException rejects the file. Consequently, upload acceptance does not guarantee that the content is a decodable image.
  • Photo validity: entity annotations require a nonblank original filename of at most 255 characters, positive nonnull file size, nonblank MIME type of at most 50 characters, and nonnull upload time. Dimensions are optional. These are declared entity constraints, not a separate controller validator.
  • Transport versus business limits: multipart configuration limits each file to 10 MB and a request to 50 MB. A configured maximum of ten files per upload is not read or enforced by the inspected controller, service, or browser code; it must not be treated as an implemented count rule.
  • Batch outcome semantics: the response success flag is true only when at least one saved Photo was read back and added to the successful summaries. Mixed success is permitted; a processed batch with only failures still returns an ordinary successful HTTP response carrying failure outcomes. A successful save with no readback result contributes to neither outcome list. There is no duplicate-filename or content-deduplication rule.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-88; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:63-106; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:33-46,85-182; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:31-82; upload and multipart properties in src/main/resources/application.properties and application-docker.properties.

Browsing, computed values, and lifecycle

  • Gallery ordering: photos are listed newest first by upload time. No pagination or search workflow is implemented.
  • Chronological navigation: previous means the nearest strictly older timestamp; next means the nearest strictly newer timestamp, additionally bounded by database current time. Equal-timestamp photos are not neighbors through these comparisons. Missing neighbors hide the corresponding navigation control.
  • Content availability: blank identities, missing photos, or absent/empty stored bytes return not-found. Unexpected retrieval or response-construction failures return a server error. Image responses discourage caching so browsers request current stored content.
  • Lifecycle: a submitted file is either rejected or becomes a stored Photo that is immediately available to the shared gallery; stored photos can be permanently removed. These are behavioral stages, not persisted status values.
  • Derived presentation: upload time and identity are assigned at construction; dimensions come from image inspection when available. Views format upload dates and byte sizes, conditionally display dimensions, and derive navigation links. No pricing, quotas per operator, or aggregate financial calculations exist.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-62; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:213-229; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:78-90; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:103-131.

Cross-cutting behavior

  • Mutation authorization: reads are public; upload and deletion POST requests require authentication. The configured account is assigned ADMIN, but the route rule checks authentication rather than that role. There is no photo ownership or per-photo permission check. Authentication uses stateless HTTP Basic; CSRF protection is disabled. No credential values are included here.
  • Transactions and integrity: PhotoServiceImpl is transactional, with read-only annotations on retrieval/navigation methods. Each upload service invocation has its own transaction; HomeController does not wrap the batch in a shared transaction. A Photo stores its metadata and bytes together, with no bidirectional domain associations to maintain. Save exceptions are caught inside the service, but deferred commit errors may propagate after method return; a caught error is not proof of a committed success.
  • Error handling: uploads use UploadResult for expected validation and handled storage errors. General retrieval/deletion failures are wrapped as runtime exceptions, then mapped by controllers to empty-gallery rendering, redirects/messages, or image-delivery errors. There are no compensating actions, dead-letter queues, or automatic business retries.
  • Audit/logging: upload acceptance/rejection, database errors, deletion, and image retrieval are logged, including photo identifiers and filenames; image-serving debug logs also include a small byte prefix. This is operational logging, not a dedicated durable business audit trail.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-28,53-74,164-208; controller failure branches cited above.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The project targets Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.5.0. The initial 3.5.0 release and the explicitly pinned Commons IO 2.14.0 warrant review against current supported maintenance releases; this build-file-only assessment does not establish lifecycle status or confirm vulnerabilities. Future major Spring Boot upgrades require checking Java baselines and framework/API compatibility. The Oracle JDBC artifact name alone does not establish Java 21 compatibility: verify the exact inherited driver version and supported Oracle database versions before modernization.

Notable Observations

  • The Spring Boot parent centralizes most versions; Commons IO is explicitly pinned outside that inherited-version pattern.
  • spring-boot-starter-json is explicitly declared alongside the web starter. It may duplicate a dependency supplied by the web starter; no transitive metadata was resolved. Despite its POM comment, it is a JSON starter, not an image-processing library.
  • DevTools is optional but has default compile scope, not runtime scope. Optionality affects downstream consumers and is not itself proof of exclusion from a deployment artifact.
  • H2 is test-only while Oracle JDBC is runtime-only; an H2 test dependency does not establish Oracle dialect or production database compatibility.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, persisted with Hibernate through Spring Data JPA. Oracle stores both photo metadata and binary image content; the test profile substitutes an in-memory H2 database.

  • Schema lifecycle: Default and Docker startup schema recreation is destructive to existing mapped data; there is no versioned migration history. Oracle initialization scripts provision and verify the database user and grants, not application tables or photo seed records (oracle-init/01-create-user.sh, oracle-init/create-user.sh, oracle-init/02-verify-user.sql).
  • Pooling: No explicit connection-pool tuning was found. HikariCP is the conventional auto-configured pool supplied transitively by the JPA starter; effective limits are framework defaults rather than repository-defined settings.
  • Seed data: No SQL photo seed scripts or programmatic database seeding were found. A bundled image under src/main/resources/static/uploads/ is a static resource, not a database seed.
  • Portability: Repository native queries use Oracle functions and pseudo-tables; the H2 profile does not configure Oracle compatibility mode. The existing context-load test does not exercise those queries (src/test/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplicationTests.java).

Key Repository Methods

All methods below belong to PhotoRepository extends JpaRepository, in src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-62. Standard inherited CRUD methods are omitted from the table; the service uses inherited lookup, save, and delete operations.

Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Native SQL returns every photo, including binary data, newest first; Oracle NVL supplies a fallback MIME type. No pagination is declared.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedBefore(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Native SQL filters older timestamps, orders descending, and limits output to ten rows with Oracle ROWNUM; supports adjacent-record lookup.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedAfter(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Native SQL filters newer timestamps up to the Oracle server's current date/time using SYSDATE and DUAL, ordered ascending; no row limit is declared.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application module owns one logical photo datastore. All photo readers and writers share PhotoRepository; there is no database-per-service split, cross-service database access, external aggregation layer, or CQRS read-model separation. H2 is a separate test database, not an additional production data owner.

Metadata and image payloads share the photos table and transactional boundary. No external object store or active filesystem-backed persistence implementation was found in the service. The entity has no uploader identifier, owner relationship, or tenant column, so row ownership and tenant isolation are not represented in the data model.
